title: One day, every register — and the way home
goal: Close a formal event with the right formulas, answer the press on the record, and then switch all the way down to the Indonesian of friends — the whole range this course has built, in a single day.
bekal: use the fixed formulas that open, hand over and close a formal event: *tibalah kita pada…, kami persilakan, demikian…*
answer journalists precisely and quotably: *bukan…, melainkan…, menurut hemat saya, sejauh ini*
move between speech, press, office and friends without a gear change showing

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Penutupan tahun pertama

notes: **Tibalah kita pada acara inti** — "we have now arrived at the main item". The inverted order (verb first, with *-lah*) is the MC's ceremonial voice; nobody talks like this at lunch, and every Indonesian recognises it at once. *Acara inti* is the main item, after the opening, prayers and national anthem.

**Kepada …, kami persilakan.** The standard hand-over to a speaker: literally "to X, we invite". The person comes first, fronted with *kepada*, and the verb *persilakan* (from *silakan*) closes the sentence. You met the pattern in Unit 13; here it is in use.

**Yang terhormat … yang saya hormati …** — the protocol ladder of a formal speech. *Yang terhormat* goes to the most senior guest (Ibu Maria, from the ministry), *yang saya hormati* to the next level. Getting the order wrong is noticed; getting it right is invisible, which is the point.

**Bukan …, melainkan …** — "not X but (rather) Y". After *bukan*, formal Indonesian prefers *melainkan* to *tetapi* for this kind of correction. It is also a perfect press answer: short, contrastive, quotable.

**Selama…, selama…** — "as long as…". Sarah repeats the frame, first serious, then comic, which is a classic Indonesian speaking move: a formal answer with a joke hidden in the second half. *Seenak sekarang* uses *se-* for "as … as": *setinggi aku* (as tall as me).

**Saya malu / saya mau.** One letter separates "I'm embarrassed" from "I'd like to", and nearly every learner has confused them at least once. Sarah's advice, *Jangan takut salah*, is the most common piece of encouragement Indonesians give learners, and they mean it.

grammars.title: Formulas that run a formal event
body: An Indonesian ceremony has a script that barely varies from Aceh to Papua. Learn these six and you can MC one yourself.

head: Formula
Job
English
rows: *Atas perhatian Bapak dan Ibu, saya ucapkan terima kasih.*

after: *Demikian* ("thus, that is all") closes speeches, letters, reports and press sessions alike. Once you hear it, you know the speaker is about to thank you and sit down.
Muslim speakers often end with *Wabillahi taufik wal hidayah, wassalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh*; in a mixed audience, add *salam sejahtera bagi kita semua*, as you learnt in Unit 13.

grammars.title: On the record: answering the press
body: Journalists want a clear sentence they can quote. These frames give you one while keeping control of what you commit to.

head: Frame
English
Use it when
rows: you want to reframe the question
the decision is not yet made

after: *Menurut hemat saya* uses *hemat* in its old sense of "careful consideration", not its everyday sense of "thrifty". It sounds modest and considered, which is why officials love it.
⚠️ *No comment* is heard as rude. *Saya belum bisa berkomentar* ("I can't comment yet") is the Indonesian equivalent; the *belum* promises that one day you will.

dialogs.intro: The same evening, in the rain, at Rina and Andi's house in South Jakarta. Kinan is six months old. Sarah arrives still in her ceremony clothes, carrying a box of martabak.

notes: **Ini dia bintang tamunya!** — "here's our guest star!" *Ini dia* ("here it/she is") greets anything long awaited: *Ini dia yang kita tunggu!* *Siaran langsung* is a live broadcast or stream.

**Jangan diungkit** — "don't bring it up". *Mengungkit* is to dig up or lever up, and figuratively to rake over something embarrassing or old. *Gemeter* is the spoken form of *gemetar* (to tremble), with the Jakarta habit of turning *-ar* into *-er*: *bener* for *benar*, *pinter* for *pintar*.

**Tante Sarah.** A close family friend becomes *Tante* (auntie, from Dutch) or *Om* (uncle) to the children, whatever the blood relationship. Rina introducing Sarah to Kinan as *Tante Sarah* is a statement: she is family now.

**Pagi “yang terhormat”, … sekarang tinggal “capek banget”.** Sarah names the registers she has used all day, from protocol to press to friends. *Tinggal* ("what remains is") is the comic drop at the end. This range, not perfection in any one of them, is what makes a speaker sound Indonesian.

**“Janji, ya!” “Pasti, dong.”** Word for word, these are the lines from the last dialogue of the A1 book, when Sarah left Jakarta for Melbourne. Rina has kept the promise in her memory for four years, and so, it turns out, has Sarah.

**Nggak pulang-pulang / aku udah pulang.** Reduplicated after a negative, *nggak pulang-pulang* means "never getting round to going home". Sarah answers with the plain verb: *pulang* is not "to return" but "to go home", so *aku udah pulang* means "I am home". Then she teaches Kinan the first words she ever learnt in the language, in a Jakarta lift, which is where this whole course began.

grammars.title: One day, four registers
body: Here is Sarah's day in one table. The same person, the same language, four different Indonesians, each exactly right for its room.
after: Nobody is taught to switch; Indonesians simply grow up doing it several times a day. If you have worked through these three books, you can now do the same, and you know why each form belongs where it does.
When in doubt, go one step more formal than you think you need. It is always easy to relax later; it is much harder to recover from being too casual too soon.

blocks.text: Indonesian has a farewell for every distance. The formal ones close events and letters; the warm ones close evenings like Sarah's.

*Dulu* in *Aku pulang dulu* does not mean "formerly" here; it means "for now, first", and softens the departure. *Saya permisi dulu* works in any setting, and is the safest leaving line in the language.
You have finished the course; the language has not finished with you. These are the habits that take a B2 speaker to the next level.
